extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy, psychology, and intellectual history; educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th‑century philosophical treatment of heredity arguing for differential parental transmission (father → will/character; mother → intellect), using introspection, historical pedigrees, and anecdotal evidence to support practical and metaphysical conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical heredity (bodily qualities)
rubrics_metrics.description: In generation the combined seed of the parents not only propagates the peculiarities of the species, but also those of the individual, as far as bodily (objective, external) qualities are concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is taken as ordinary, uncontroversial experience and the basis for further discussion of mental heredity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental heredity (general claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether mental (subjective, internal) qualities are also transmitted by the parents to the children is a frequently raised question, and almost always answered in the affirmative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author treats mental heredity as plausible and worth examining through examples and argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paternal transmission: will and moral character
rubrics_metrics.description: Assumes the father, as sexus potior and the procreative principle, imparts the basis, the radical element of the new life — thus the will, moral nature, character, inclinations, and heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by introspective comparisons and historical family pedigrees; tempered by caveats (see 'paternity uncertainty' and maternal modification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maternal transmission: intellect and cognitive faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: Assumes the mother, as sexus sequior and merely conceiving principle, imparts the secondary element — the intellect (grade, quality, and tendency of intelligence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author cites the popular expression 'mother‑wit' and many examples (Buffon, Goethe, Kant, etc.) and notes that maternal intellect is often less publicly visible due to social constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: introspective/personal comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary evidence: refer every one to his own experience — consider oneself and compare inclinations, passions, characteristic errors, and virtues with those of the father and mother.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful, candid, attentive comparison of specific traits (e.g., temper, avarice, courage) is proposed as strong evidence for paternal/maternal inheritance patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: historical pedigrees as evidence (with caveats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical examples are useful because they are universally known, but are impaired by uncertainty, falsification, and focus on public rather than private life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical pedigrees (e.g., gens Fabia, Scipios, Borgia, Nero) as corroborating evidence but recognize their limits and possible bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paternity uncertainty as a limiting condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Two inevitable limitations: first, 'pater semper incertus' — only a decided physical resemblance to the father removes this limitation; second, the father's moral character may appear modified by the mother's intellect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing paternal inheritance, account for possible uncertainty of biological paternity and the after-effects of prior impregnations observed in animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maternal intellectual modification of paternal passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when paternal passions are inherited, they are modified by the intellect inherited from the mother (e.g., bridled, concealed, made methodical or secret).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect hybrid manifestations: the father's passions may appear differently depending on maternal intellectual inheritance (degree and kind of reason).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation for occurrence (genius requires both inputs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Great genius generally requires both an extraordinarily developed brain (maternal contribution) and a very energetic action of the heart (paternal contribution); both appropriate timing and parental health at conception matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why genius is rare, why elder children often excel, and why parental age/health/temporary states at conception can alter outcomes (twins and eldest vs younger siblings discussed).

rubrics_metrics.name: On sibling similarity and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sons of the same mother tend to have equal mental capacity, but exceptions occur due to physiological conditions at conception, differences in the father's contribution, or other disturbing factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sibling comparisons (e.g., Carracci, Haydn brothers) but allow for exceptions (Kant's brother) and explain via prior chapter physiological conditions of genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility bias in assessing maternal inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: Maternal intellectual qualities are often underrepresented in history because women's social role and weaker general physique limited public achievements, so maternal influence may be underestimated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust assessments of maternal transmission to account for social suppression of female public accomplishment; the mother's faculties may be transmitted and amplified in sons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific claim: certain maladies more often maternal
rubrics_metrics.description: According to Esquirol and other authorities, madness is more frequently inherited from the mother than from the father.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat claims about differential transmission of disease (e.g., insanity) as part of the hereditary picture; infer possible maternal line transmission while considering alternative dispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anthropological/ethical implication: incest prohibition rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: The incest taboo (brother‑sister marriage forbidden) may be rooted in the adaptive disadvantage that such unions would produce the same will with the same intellect (no renewal of intellect for the same will).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This offers an ethico‑metaphysical argument linking heredity theory to social norms: sexual separation preserves variation necessary for 'salvation' or development of will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy/procedural proposals based on heredity claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical applications suggested include preferring dowries to the most intelligent girls rather than the supposedly most virtuous, considering reproductive selection to improve the race, and abolishing burdens (head‑carrying) that harm female brains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These policy proposals flow from the premise that maternal intellect shapes national intelligence; they are presented as speculative/practical consequences rather than settled prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemic humility: limits of causal explanation for character
rubrics_metrics.description: There remain cases where the principle of sufficient reason fails when explaining the will as thing‑in‑itself; some differences of character cannot be reduced to heredity or causal genealogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge metaphysical limits: certain aspects of individual character may be grounded in the thing‑in‑itself (will) and thus resist explanation by hereditary mechanism.
